stops.name: Zaragoza, birth at the Aljafería
stops.campa: Yolande is born in the Moorish-towered palace of the Aljafería, eldest surviving daughter of Juan I of Aragon and Violant de Bar, a mother who carries in her own blood the county that, a lifetime away in Lorraine, holds the Bourlémont lords of Domrémy in vassalage. The Aragonese court under her father is a court of music, astrology and courtly love, and the infanta grows fluent in Occitan song before she is fluent in statecraft. No one yet calls her Queen of Four Kingdoms; she is only a daughter, and Aragon already needs a son.

stops.name: Zaragoza, the betrothal to Louis of Anjou
stops.campa: At nine years old Yolande is promised to Louis II of Anjou, titular king of Sicily and Jerusalem, a match brokered by his mother Marie of Blois against the ambitions of half of Christendom. Richard II of England will later try to claim her for himself, and Charles VI of France will head him off by offering his own daughter instead. The Aragonese match holds. It binds a princess of the house that will lose Aragon to a house that will never truly sit any of its four crowns, and win, instead, the whole of France.

stops.name: Foixà, the death of King Juan I
stops.campa: Hunting near Foixà in the forests of the Empordà, Yolande's father is thrown from his horse and dies within the hour, leaving no surviving son. The crown of Aragon passes to his brother Martín, and then, after Martín dies without heir, to a foreign Castilian prince chosen at Caspe, never to Yolande, never to her line, though she and her sons will go on calling themselves kings and queens of Aragon into the next generation. She is fourteen. The lesson she draws, that a throne unheld by force is a throne merely claimed, will outlast her father by fifty years.

stops.name: Arles, marriage to Louis II at Saint-Trophime
stops.campa: In the Romanesque nave of Saint-Trophime at Arles, under the carved apostles of the west portal, Yolande is married to Louis II of Anjou: Duke of Anjou, Count of Provence, titular King of Sicily, Naples and Jerusalem. She is nineteen; the marriage that seemed for years about to fail on money and politics is at last made. She becomes at a stroke Duchess of Anjou, Countess of Provence and Maine, and titular queen of three kingdoms she will never see crowned in. The fourth, Aragon, is already lost to her by an accident of birth.

stops.name: Angers, the castle on the Maine
stops.campa: The young duchess comes north to Angers, the great black-and-white striped fortress of seventeen towers above the river Maine, and makes it, with Saumur upriver, the true seat of her house, more than any court in Provence or Naples. Here she will bear five children, bury a husband, raise a king's bride, shelter a king, and govern in all but name for thirty years. The Angevin tapestry of the Apocalypse already hangs in these halls, woven a generation before her arrival: dragons and angels she will come, in her own way, to resemble.

stops.name: Tarascon, the family castle on the Rhône
stops.campa: Downriver from Avignon the house of Anjou-Provence holds the castle of Tarascon on its rock above the Rhône, patroness-town of Saint Martha, who by the old legend bound and tamed the man-eating Tarasque here with nothing but holy water and a girdle. The Angevin court keeps Martha's cult alive in the town below walls Yolande's family will one day rebuild in stone. She summers here among troubadour song and olive terraces, the same Provençal ground where, two centuries before, another Bourlémont daughter learned the gaya ciencia in a cousin household of the same Rhône valley world.

stops.name: Angers, birth of Louis III
stops.campa: Yolande's first child, Louis, is born at Angers on the twenty-fifth of September, heir to the duchy of Anjou and, on paper, to the crown of Naples his father is already fighting to make real. He will grow to be adopted by Queen Giovanna II of Naples as her own son and heir, carrying the Angevin claim to Italy that his mother will spend the next three decades financing, defending, and watching consume itself in Neapolitan politics far from the France she is quietly coming to govern instead.

stops.name: Angers, birth of Marie, future queen of France
stops.campa: A second child, Marie, is born at Angers a little over a year after her brother. No one yet knows she is being raised for the throne of France; the girl who will one day marry the dauphin Charles is, for now, simply a duchess's daughter learning her letters in the Angevin nursery. Yolande will spend the next nine years engineering exactly that marriage, reading the wreck of the mad king's court with the patience of a woman who has already lost one kingdom and does not intend to lose the next.

stops.name: Aix-en-Provence, the comital court and the troubadours
stops.campa: At Aix, seat of the counts of Provence, Yolande keeps a second court in the old troubadour tongue, where jongleurs and singers of the gaya ciencia still perform the canso and the alba her Provençal in-laws have patronized for two centuries. She holds both languages of her life here at once, the hard Aragonese statecraft of her father's house and the ornamental, love-sick Provençal culture of her husband's, and raises her children between them, a bilingualism of politics and poetry that her son René will carry to its furthest, strangest flowering.

stops.name: Angers, birth of René
stops.campa: A second son, René, is born at Angers on the sixteenth of January. He will be fostered out young to the Lorraine court of Cardinal Louis of Bar and Duke Charles II, learning to joust and illuminate manuscripts in the household of the very family whose county holds, in law, the Bourlémont lords of Domrémy and their overlordship of a girl not yet born who will one day be Yolande's most consequential discovery. Of all her children, René is the one who will carry the house's strange, ornamental, occult-tinged afterlife into the next century as a poet-king.

stops.name: Provence, regent while Louis fights for Naples
stops.campa: While Louis campaigns in Italy against Ladislaus of Naples, Yolande governs as his lieutenant-general in Anjou and Provence, empowered to act in every capacity for her absent husband. When rebels in Provence try the old trick of striking while the duke is away, she does not send for him: she raises an army herself and puts the revolt down before it can spread, managing finances, defenses and the fractious Provençal nobility with a hand that surprises men who expected a duchess to wait quietly at her needlework for her husband's return.

stops.name: Angers, birth of Yolande of Anjou
stops.campa: A fourth child, named Yolande for her mother, is born at Angers. She will grow to marry Francis, Count of Montfort: one more thread of the vast marriage-web her mother weaves across thirty years to bind Anjou to Brittany, to Lorraine, to the crown of France itself, each child a treaty in the making. The duchess raises her daughters, as she raises her sons, to understand that a good marriage negotiated early is worth more than an army raised late.
